name: Permutation Problem (Simple Version)
description: This is a simple version of the problem. The only difference is that in this version $$$n \leq 10^5$$$ and the sum of $$$n$$$ for all sets of input data does not exceed $$$10^5$$$. You are given a permutation $$$p$$$ of length $$$n$$$. Calculate the number of index pairs $$$1 \leq i \lt j \leq n$$$ such that $$$p_i \cdot p_j$$$ is divisible by $$$i \cdot j$$$ without remainder. A permutation is a sequence of $$$n$$$ integers, where each integer from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ occurs exactly once. For example, $$$[1]$$$, $$$[3,5,2,1,4]$$$, $$$[1,3,2]$$$ are permutations, while $$$[2,3,2]$$$, $$$[4,3,1]$$$, $$$[0]$$$ are not.
input_specification: Each test consists of multiple sets of input data. The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of sets of input data. Then follows their description. The first line of each set of input data contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$) — the length of the permutation $$$p$$$. The second line of each set of input data contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq n$$$) — the permutation $$$p$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ for all sets of input data does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each set of input data, output the number of index pairs $$$1 \leq i \lt j \leq n$$$ such that $$$p_i \cdot p_j$$$ is divisible by $$$i \cdot j$$$ without remainder.
approach_summary: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to N using Fermat's Little Theorem (mod 10^9+7 or 998244353). Answer nCr queries in O(1) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1986G1 — Permutation Problem (Simple Version) [310. Large Factorials and Binomial Coefficients]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Combinatorial selection $\binom{N}{K} = \frac{N!}{K!(N-K)!} \pmod P$ can be evaluated in $O(1)$ by precomputing factorials $fact[i] = fact[i-1] \cdot i \pmod P$ and inverse factorials $invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] \cdot (i+1) \pmod P$ using Fermat's Little Theorem $a^{P-2} \equiv a^{-1} \pmod P$.
